source: In the S bus, in the rush hour. A chap of about 26, felt hat with a cord instead of a ribbon, neck too long, as if someone’s been having a tug-of-war with it. People getting off. The chap in question gets annoyed with one of the men standing next to him. He accuses him of jostling him every time anyone goes past. A snivelling tone which is meant to be aggressive. When he sees a vacant seat he throws himself on to it. Two hours later, I meet him in the Cour de Rome, in front of the gare Saint-Lazare. He’s with a friend who’s saying: "You ought to get an extra button put on your overcoat." He shows him where (at the lapels) and why.

gens.text: In the Mercy ward, at the crush hour. A patient of around forty, hospital gown with a clip instead of a tie, wrist too swollen, as though somebody had been tightening a strap on it. Beds shifting. The patient in distress snaps at one of the nurses hovering nearby. He blames her for ignoring him whenever a doctor passes. A whining tone which reads as furious. When he spots an empty gurney he wheels toward it. Ninety minutes later, I glimpse him near the Radiology Suite, before the Central Registration Desk. He’s beside an attendant who’s urging: "You really should have a fresh bracelet clamped on your wrist." He indicates where and why.

Inside the Mercy ward, at the busy hour. A patient of maybe thirty, sweating despite the chill, jaw clenched tight, as though somebody were tightening a vise on it, gripping a slip while a nurse hurries past him. Monitors chirp. The patient beside the curtain snaps at one of the orderlies wheeling gurneys. He blames him for stalling every intake ahead of him. A wheezing whine that sounds like pleading. He grabs it whenever he spots a free wristband someone abandoned. Ninety minutes afterward, I glimpse him near the pharmacy, outside the East Annex. He's with a woman who is telling him to bring the discharge papers signed by his physician. She waves them right at him, then here.

In the County ER, at the peak surge. A woman around forty, hospital gown with a clip instead of a tie, wrist too pale, as if someone had been draining color from it. Patients arriving. When she spots an empty gurney she lunges onto it. Three hours later, I glimpse her near the Radiology wing, outside the Emory Imaging Suite. She's beside a nurse who is murmuring: "You should have another wristband scanned for identification." He points where (at the arm) and how.
